RECOMMENDATION
Conduct a public hearing and upon conclusion:
   1. Adopt first reading of an Ordinance repealing and reenacting Berkeley Municipal
      Code chapter 14.52, “Parking Meters,” to enable the following changes:
          a. Extend parking meter operating hours to 8 p.m. citywide;
          b. Operate parking meters, pay stations, and parking enforcement on
              Sundays.
          c. Expand meter zones to new high-demand areas (refer to Attachment 1,
              Exhibit A);
          d. Authorize a transition to cashless parking meters and/or pay stations in
              the future; and
   2. Adopt a Resolution to pass through parking meter costs currently paid by the
      City to a transparent transaction charge paid by the customer; and
   3. Adopt a Resolution implementing a new FY 2028 fee schedule for Residential
      Parking Permit fees; and
   4. Adopt a Resolution updating the Schedule of Parking Violations and Fines; and
      rescinding Resolution No. 71,627-N.S. (Parking Violations and Fines).

SUMMARY
Following the implementation of near-term strategies in March and April 2026, the
Public Works Department has identified that further adjustments are necessary to
update fees and citation amounts to keep pace with City costs to administer parking
programs. Such changes will also serve to manage parking in high-demand commercial
districts, and to improve the solvency of the Off-Street and Parking Meter Funds. These
changes align with the City’s goals for the goBerkeley Parking Management Program,
including:

      1) Making it easier to find a parking space near popular destinations;

CURRENT SITUATION AND ITS EFFECTS
This report covers three primary changes to the City’s parking program:
   1. Adjustments to the goBerkeley program to address parking demand, modernize
       parking infrastructure, and reduce operational costs;
   2. Updates to the Residential Parking Permit fees to cover City costs from
       administering the program and to reflect the City’s environmental priorities; and
   3. Updates to the Schedule of Parking Violations and Fines.

goBerkeley Adjustments
When combined, the City’s Parking Meter and Off-Street Parking Funds are currently
facing a projected structural deficit, necessitating a transition toward more sustainable
and technologically modern management models. Recent data indicates that parking
demand in Berkeley’s commercial cores remains high during evenings and on
Sundays—periods when meters are currently inactive. This lack of active management
results in high occupancy, which discourages vehicle turnover, harms local business
access, and increases "cruising" for spaces, a major contributor to localized traffic
congestion and greenhouse gas emissions.

Furthermore, the operational maintenance of the City's aging parking infrastructure is
increasingly inefficient; mechanical coin operators and receipt printers are the primary



                                                    Page 6
                                               Page 7 of 518

point of failure for pay stations, and the manual collection of physical currency requires
significant staff resources and armored transport costs. Currently, the City absorbs
credit card processing fees for every transaction through a parking meter, which directly
erodes the net revenue of the Parking Meter Fund and is inconsistent with the
customer-paid “convenience fee” model used by the City’s mobile parking vendor,
ParkMobile. By extending meter hours, expanding zones to unmanaged high-demand
areas, and transitioning to a cashless, transparent cost-based model, the City can
reduce operational overhead, stabilize the parking funds, and ensure that the cost of
curb management is borne by users rather than being subsidized.

The revenue generated from parking meters is no longer sufficient to fully cover the
costs of the Police Department’s Parking Enforcement unit, including the maintenance
of enforcement vehicles, cost of labor, costs of License Plate Recognition (LPR)
technology, Public Works operational costs, or the annual debt service costs
(approximately $1.9 million) for the Center Street Garage reconstruction. Increasing
revenue for the Parking Meter Fund provides the necessary cost recovery to maintain a
robust parking management program.

Regional and National Comparison
San Francisco operates the most robust evening and weekend program in the region,
with meters in high-traffic zones like Fisherman's Wharf and the Embarcadero running
until 10 p.m. and on Sundays. Walnut Creek also operates meters until 8 p.m., including
Sundays; and Oakland began operating parking meters on Sundays in January 2026.
Outside of the Bay Area, other cities such as Sacramento, Los Angeles, Seattle,
Washington D.C., and Chicago operate parking meters until 8 p.m. or later.

Equity Considerations
To mitigate potential barriers for unbanked or underbanked individuals who may be
inconvenienced by the transition to a cashless parking environment, the new cashless
pay stations would integrate Clipper card functionality into all new tap-to-pay parking
hardware. Because Clipper cards can be replenished with physical currency at
numerous retail locations and Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) stations, they serve as a
vital "cash-to-digital" bridge. This approach preserves the operational benefits of a
cashless system—such as eliminating mechanical coin- or printer-jams and reducing
manual cash processing costs—while ensuring that the public right-of-way remains
accessible to all community members, regardless of their access to traditional banking
or credit services.

Currently, the City employs five full-time staff members as parking meter collectors who
are responsible for the collection and processing of cash from nearly 2,200 meters and
pay stations. As the program transitions to cashless technology over a projected three-
to-five-year period, these job descriptions will evolve to reflect the diminishing need for
manual cash handling. If Public Works observes that these positions are no longer

Residential Parking Permit Fees
The Residential Parking Permit Program (RPP) was established to protect
neighborhood quality of life, yet it currently faces a significant funding gap. Total
program expenses are driven primarily by the personnel costs of 21 Parking
Enforcement Officers and 3 supervisors, as well as administrative staff from Public
Works, Finance, and the 311 call center. Total RPP expenses are estimated at
approximately $4.12 million annually. Historically, however, RPP revenue, including
citation revenue in RPP zones, has averaged only $2.85 million, leaving an estimated
$1.3 million deficit that must be subsidized by the Parking Meter Fund and General
Fund. Clearly, the fee structure must be modernized to reflect the true costs to the City
of administering the Residential Parking Permit Program.

The current "flat-fee" structure also fails to address the environmental and equity
impacts of excessive vehicle storage on public streets. Households that utilize the public
right-of-way for three or more vehicles currently pay the same per-permit rate as those
with only one vehicle, despite occupying a disproportionate amount of limited curb
space. By transitioning to a graduated fee scale—where the first permit is more
affordable than the 3rd permit for vehicles at a single address—the City can encourage
residents to utilize off-street parking where available, reduce the "privatization" of public
space for long-term car storage, and move the RPP program closer to its goal of being
a self-supporting enterprise.

The recommended fee increases (see Table 3 on following page) would go into effect
on May 1, 2027, the first day residents can purchase their FY 2028 RPP permits.

Schedule of Parking Violations and Fines
The City’s Schedule of Parking Violations and Fines has not been comprehensively
adjusted to keep pace with the rising costs of enforcement and regional inflation. While
minor modifications to the schedule have been made recently based on changes to the
California Vehicle Code, the fine amounts for some of the most common citations—such
as expired meters or street sweeping—have not been increased in over 15 years.
Currently, the City’s fine amounts for many common violations are significantly lower
than those of neighboring jurisdictions, which diminishes the deterrent effect of a
citation. For example, a citation for an expired meter in Berkeley is currently $43,
whereas the same violation is $64 in Oakland and as high as $108 in high-demand
areas of San Francisco. Similarly, Berkeley’s street sweeping fine is $49, compared to
$72 in Oakland and $97 in San Francisco. As shown in Attachment 4, Exhibit A, the
recommendation herein would increase the City’s parking fines commensurate with
cumulative inflation that has occurred since the last time each parking fine was
increased. For most violation types, the last update was in 2010, and each of these
fines are increased by 49%. However, some violation types were added to the Schedule
of Parking Violations and Fines more recently, for example in 2012, 2018, 2023, and
2024, and therefore these fine amounts are increased by less. Increasing fine amounts
to keep pace with inflation results in increases of between 3% to 49%, or in practical

Public Outreach/Survey
In early March 2026, the City released a public survey regarding potential adjustments
to the parking management program, which was accompanied by a community
message released by the City’s Communications team. The survey received 669
responses, equivalent to 33.5 hours of public comment. The survey results are included
as Attachment 5 and summarized below.

A majority of respondents (over 50%) expressed agreement or strong agreement with
each of the core objectives of the goBerkeley program, specifically:
    Improving parking availability near popular destinations.
    Reducing greenhouse gas emissions by decreasing vehicle "circling."
    Increasing vehicle turnover to support local economic vitality and merchant
      access.
    Enhancing safety for pedestrians and cyclists by reducing double-parking and
      distracted driving.

Feedback regarding proposed operational shifts was more closely divided, with
sentiment leaning toward opposition for the following:
    Evening Meter Hours: 53% oppose vs. 36% support.
    Sunday Operations: 49% oppose vs. 43% support.
    Geographic Expansion: 44% oppose vs. 38% support.

There is decisive public support for infrastructure updates; 70% of respondents favor
the transition to Tap-to-Pay hardware and the integration of Clipper cards as a cash-
accessible alternative, while 17% are opposed.

Respondents showed moderate support for cost transparency, with 47% in favor and
33% opposed to the proposal for a transparent $0.25–$0.35 service charge.

Overall, managing parking demand and ensuring the solvency of the parking funds is
consistent with the City’s Strategic Plan, advancing our goals to provide state-of-the-art,
well-maintained infrastructure, amenities, and facilities; and to provide an efficient and
financially healthy City government.

BACKGROUND
The City’s parking management program includes three main components

    1. goBerkeley: the data-driven, demand-responsive parking management program
       consisting of parking meters in commercial areas, three City-owned garages, and
       two surface parking lots: one in the Elmwood district and the other near the
       intersection of Alcatraz Ave and Adeline Street;




                                                   Page 11
                                              Page 12 of 518

                                                                              June 9, 2026


    2. The Residential Parking Permit Program: a neighborhood management
       system designed to prioritize curb space for residents and/or their caretakers,
       merchants, and institutional employees while protecting neighborhoods from
       overwhelming parking demand from visitors or commuters; and

    3. Parking Enforcement: a dedicated team of 21 specialized officers, two
       supervisors, and one manager who utilizes License Plate Recognition technology
       in parking enforcement vehicles to systematically monitor and enforce parking
       regulations.

goBerkeley Adjustments
The goBerkeley Parking Program was established to manage the City’s limited curb
space through demand-responsive pricing, ensuring that residents, visitors, and
customers can find available parking in or near commercial districts. On January 27,
2026, the City Council approved a series of "near-term" strategies—implemented on
March 1, 2026, for on-street meters and April 1, 2026, for City garages—to start to
address a structural deficit in the Parking Meter Fund (631) and the Off-Street Parking
Fund (627). Despite these initial adjustments, both funds remain under pressure due to
the high cost of maintaining aging hardware and the evolving driving patterns of a post-
pandemic economy.

Currently, the City operates approximately 1,945 single-space meters and 242 multi-
space pay stations. These aging units frequently require mechanical repairs due to
printer and coin jams; and the manual collection of physical currency requires
specialized personnel and secure transport. Transitioning to a cashless system
represents the next phase of the goBerkeley roadmap, aimed at reducing "down-time"
and unnecessary cost.

Parking meters are a strategy for managing the curb as a finite public resource. The
goBerkeley program has been extended to different hours of the day and new
commercial areas in the past where parking availability and turnover are critical for
customer access and convenience. As shown in Attachment 1, Exhibit A, in the
absence of pricing, many blocks without meters exceed 85% occupancy during the day,
which effectively blocks access for short-term visitors, delivery drivers, and customers.
Introducing meters encourages vehicle turnover, ensuring that a consistent number of
spaces (one to two per block) remain available throughout the day. This improved
accessibility is vital for the economic health of a district, as it significantly reduces
"cruising," the process where drivers circle blocks searching for parking. Cruising is a
major contributor to localized traffic congestion and greenhouse gas emissions. By
pricing the curb to match demand, the City can decrease unnecessary vehicle miles
traveled while ensuring that the public right-of-way supports the needs of local
businesses and the environment.

Residential Parking Permit Fees
The RPP program was instituted in 1980 to: protect City residential neighborhoods from
an influx of non-resident vehicles and related traffic; and to assure continued quality of
life for residents. The RPP program limits parking for vehicles without valid permits in
most areas to two hours and reserves available daytime parking for residents or other
permit-holders, from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Friday, and on some blocks,
Saturday.

On June 24, 2025, City Council approved increasing RPP Program fees for the FY 2027
permit year to make progress in addressing the gap between RPP Program revenue
and expenses (Resolution No. 71,839-N.S. Regarding Preferential Parking Program
Permit Fees). However, to achieve full cost recovery and align with the City’s
environmental goals, a more sophisticated structure is required. The proposed
graduated fee scale for FY 2028 recognizes that the public right-of-way is a finite
resource; by increasing the cost for households with three or more vehicles, the City
seeks to encourage the use of off-street parking and reduce the long-term storage of
private vehicles on public streets, thereby supporting Berkeley's Climate Action Plan
goals.

Schedule of Parking Violations and Fines
Parking fines and late penalties are a critical tool for ensuring compliance with the City’s
parking regulations and recovering the cost of administering the City’s parking
programs. Berkeley’s fine schedule has remained largely static for the last 15 years
while nearby cities have adjusted theirs to account for inflation and the rising costs of
enforcement equipment, including vehicles and License Plate Reader technology.

The current fine for an expired meter in Berkeley ($43) is significantly lower than in
Oakland ($64) or San Francisco (up to $108), creating a "compliance gap" where the
financial penalty is no longer a sufficient deterrent against overstaying time limits. This
leads to reduced compliance with parking regulations and lower parking revenue
collection.

ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE IMPACTS
In general, parking supports driving by dedicating curb space to car storage rather than
alternative modes such as transit, walking, or biking. Free parking encourages overuse,
while charging fees for parking and enforcing parking regulations are the most effective
ways to manage demand. Lower demand for parking signals fewer vehicle trips overall,
resulting in reduced fuel consumption and congestion caused by drivers circling the
block searching for parking. Moreover, fewer vehicle trips represents a shift toward
sustainable alternatives such as walking, biking, or taking public transit, which improves
air quality and lowers greenhouse gas emissions.

This action is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) under
CEQA Guidelines § 15301 because the proposed adjustments to the goBerkeley

Parking Management Program, including extending meter hours, initiating Sunday

the parking violations schedule, and authorizing a transition to cashless parking meters,
involve the operation, maintenance, and minor alteration of existing public facilities
(including parking meters, pay stations, signage, and curbside regulations) without
expanding their physical footprint or capacity. Further, as regulatory measures designed
to maintain and protect environmental resources by reducing vehicle circling, lowering
greenhouse gas emissions, and improving curbside management, these changes are
also exempt under CEQA Guidelines § 15307 (Actions by Regulatory Agencies for
Protection of Natural Resources). Additionally, the program updates constitute
regulatory actions intended to ensure proper enforcement of parking regulations,
improve compliance, and reduce environmental and traffic impacts, which are
categorically exempt under §15308 (Actions by Regulatory Agencies for Protection of
the Environment).

RATIONALE FOR RECOMMENDATION
This recommendation would align parking meter and permit fees with the cost of
administering the Parking Management Program and the Residential Parking Permit
programs, respectively. These strategies would ensure program costs are adequately
covered including capital renewal and debt service. Without these measures, the City
would not be able to administer these programs effectively because the combined
parking fund balance is projected to be in deficit by approximately $1,000,000 at the end
of FY 2027. As shown in Figure 1, above, with implementation of these measures, the
combined Parking Fund balance is projected to be about $1,610,000 by the end of FY
2027.

ALTERNATIVE ACTIONS CONSIDERED
Staff considered other strategies such as advertising opportunities and reusing garages
for other uses besides parking but determined these strategies would require additional
personnel or capital investment and will be explored further in the future. Staff continue
to evaluate the parking programs and their assets and expect to bring periodic
recommendations to Council in the future.

C. The City Traffic Engineer shall cause parking meters and pay stations to be installed

14.52.020 Manner of installation.

A. Single space meters.

1. Parking meters shall be installed upon the curb or sidewalk area immediately
adjacent to each parking space. Each meter shall be placed in such manner as to show
or display by a sign or signal that the parking space adjacent thereto is or is not legally
in use. Each parking meter shall indicate the limit of parking time in the parking space
adjacent to the parking meter.

2. Each parking meter shall be set to display, after the operational procedure has been
completed, a sign or signal indicating legal parking for that period of time conforming to
the limit of parking time as indicated on the meter, and shall continue to operate from
the time of the completion of the operational procedure until the expiration of the time
fixed as the parking limit or a portion thereof for the part of the street upon which said
meter is placed. Each said meter shall also be so arranged that upon the expiration of
said legal parking time it will indicate by a mechanical operation and by proper signal
that the lawful parking period has expired.

B. Pay stations.

1. Pay stations are used to accept payment for multiple paid parking spaces on a block
face or off-street parking lot and shall include pay-and-display stations and pay-by-plate
stations.

2. Pay stations shall be installed upon the curb or sidewalk area within any designated
meter zone. Each pay station shall indicate the limit of parking time in that particular
designated meter zone.

3. Each pay-and-display station shall be set to dispense, after the operational
procedure has been completed, a two-part windshield dispensing machine ticket
indicating legal parking for that period of time conforming to the limit of parking time as
indicated on the pay-and-display station or indicated by signage or curb markings.

4. Each pay-by-plate station shall be set for the vehicle operator to register their vehicle
license plate as the parking permit indicating legal parking for that period of time
conforming to the limit of parking time as indicated on the pay-by-plate station or
indicated by signage or curb markings.

14.52.030 Time of operation of parking meters and pay stations.
                                      Page 25 of 518




A. The provision of this chapter relating to the operation of parking meters and pay
stations shall be effective between the hours of nine a.m. and eight p.m. every day, and
as may be otherwise provided for specific locations in the sections of establishing
parking meter zones.

B. goBerkeley SmartSpace Program

1. The provision of this chapter relating to the operation of parking meters and pay
stations in the goBerkeley SmartSpace program areas listed in 14.52.010 (B) shall be
effective between the hours of eight a.m. and eight p.m. every day.

2. A motor vehicle which has a valid RPP “Area I” annual or visitor residential parking
permit is exempt from hourly paid parking in the goBerkeley SmartSpace program areas
listed in 14.52.010 (B).


14.52.040 Operational procedure to be followed.

A. Single space meters. Immediately after occupancy of a parking meter space, the
operator of a vehicle shall, if necessary, deposit a coin of the United States, or use a
credit or debit card acceptable to the City, or use a tap-to-pay enabled device, or use a
City-approved software application that processes pay-by-phone payments from a
mobile phone, at said parking meter in accordance with the instructions posted on the
face of the parking meter or the pay-by-phone software application that processes
payments from a mobile device.

B. Pay-and-display stations.

1. Immediately after occupancy of a pay-and-display station space, the operator of a
vehicle shall, if necessary, locate the nearest pay-and-display station on the block and
deposit a coin of the United States, or use a credit or debit card acceptable to the City,
or use a tap-to-pay enabled device, or use a City-approved software application that
processes pay-by-phone payments from a mobile phone at said pay-and-display station
and make selections in accordance with the instructions posted on the face of the pay-
and-display station, or the pay-by-phone software application that processes payments
from a mobile phone.

2. Upon obtaining the printed dispensing machine ticket from the pay-and-display
station, the operator of the vehicle shall return immediately to their vehicle and place the
dispensing machine ticket face up on the street-side of the vehicle’s dashboard in such
a manner that the expiration time and date are readily visible from the exterior.

C. Pay-by-plate stations.
                                      Page 26 of 518




Immediately after occupancy of a pay-by-plate station space, the operator of a vehicle
shall, if necessary, locate the nearest pay-by-plate station on the block, enter their
vehicle license plate number to register their payment, deposit a coin of the United
States, or use a credit or debit card acceptable to the City, or use a tap-to-pay enabled
device, or use a City-approved software application that processes pay-by-phone
payments from a mobile phone at said pay-by-plate station, and make selections in
accordance with the instructions posted on the face of the pay-by-plate station, or the
pay-by-phone software application that processes payments from a mobile phone.


14.52.050 Unlawful to park after meter and/or pay station time has expired.

A. Single space meter. It is unlawful for the operator of any vehicle to permit said
vehicle to remain parked in any parking space during any time that an operable meter is
showing a signal indicating that such space is illegally in use, such as where the time
has expired, unless the operator of the vehicle has otherwise paid for the parking space
via the use of a City-approved software application that processes pay-by-phone
payments from a mobile phone, other than such time immediately after the original
occupancy as is necessary to operate the meter to show legal parking.

B. Pay-and-display stations. It is unlawful for the operator of any vehicle to permit said
vehicle to remain parked in any parking space during any time that pay-and-display
station dispensing machine ticket is indicating that such space is illegally in use, such as
where the time has expired, unless the operator of the vehicle has otherwise paid for
the parking space via the use of a City-approved software application that processes
pay-by-phone payments from a mobile phone, other than such time immediately after
the original occupancy as is necessary to obtain a receipt from the pay-and-display
station and to place said dispensing machine ticket face up on the street-side of the
vehicle’s dashboard to show legal parking.

C. Pay-by plate stations. It is unlawful for the operator of any vehicle to permit said
vehicle to remain parked in any parking space during any time that the operator has not
registered their vehicle by entering their vehicle license plate number and submitted
payment at the nearest pay-by-plate station, unless the operator of the vehicle has
otherwise paid for the parking space via the use of a City-approved software application
that processes pay-by-phone payments from a mobile phone, other than such time
immediately after the original occupancy as is necessary to register their vehicle license
plate number at the pay-by-plate station.

14.52.060 Unlawful to extend time beyond limit.

A. Single space meter. It is unlawful and a violation of the provisions of this chapter for
any person to follow the operational procedure or any part of the operational procedure
for the purpose of increasing or extending the parking time of any vehicle beyond the
                                      Page 27 of 518




legal parking time which has been established for the parking space adjacent to which
said parking meter is placed.

B. Pay-and-display stations. It is unlawful and a violation of the provisions of this
chapter for any person to follow the operational procedure or any part of the operational
procedure for the purpose of increasing or extending the parking time of any vehicle
beyond the legal parking time which has been established for the parking space which
is indicated on the pay-and-display station dispensing machine ticket.

C. Pay-by-plate stations. It is unlawful and a violation of the provisions of this chapter for
any person to follow the operational procedure or any part of the operational procedure
for the purpose of increasing or extending the parking time of any vehicle beyond the
legal parking time which has been established for the parking space controlled by the
nearest pay-by-plate station.

14.52.063 No pay-and-display dispensing machine ticket displayed.
A motor vehicle on which is properly displayed a valid pay-and-display dispensing
machine ticket as provided for herein shall be permitted to stand or be parked in a pay-
and-display zone for which the dispensing machine ticket has been issued for the period
of time indicated on the dispensing machine ticket without being subject to parking
penalties in effect for such area. However, any motor vehicle on which there is not
displayed a valid dispensing machine ticket as provided herein shall be subject to
parking regulations and consequent penalties in effect for such area. (Ord. 7305-NS
(part), 2013)

14.52.066 Improperly displayed pay-and-display dispensing machine ticket.
A motor vehicle on which the pay-and-display dispensing machine ticket is not properly
displayed as provided herein shall be subject to parking regulations and consequent
penalties in effect for such area. (Ord. 7305-NS (part), 2013)

14.52.070 Improper use of meter and pay station.
It is unlawful to deposit or cause to be deposited in any parking meter any defaced or
bent coin, or any slug, device or metallic substitute for a coin of the United States, or to
otherwise use any card or other device in a parking meter or pay station having
alternative payment capability in lieu of a card or device lawful and appropriate to an
alternative payment process at such parking meter or pay station, or for any person to
deface, injure, tamper with, open or willfully break, destroy or impair the usefulness of
any parking meter or pay station. (Ord. 7305-NS (part), 2013)

14.52.080 Deposit of coins in meter or coins, credit card, debit card, or epark card
in meter or pay station by unauthorized person.

A. Single space meter. It is unlawful for any person, other than the owner or operator of
a vehicle, to deposit any coin, debit card or credit card in any parking meter without the
                                      Page 28 of 518




knowledge or consent of said owner or operator of the vehicle using the parking space
immediately adjacent to said meter.

B. Pay stations. It is unlawful for any person, other than the owner or operator of a
vehicle, to deposit any coin, credit card, debit card, or epark card in any pay station
without the knowledge or consent of said owner or operator of the vehicle using the
parking space. (Ord. 7305-NS (part), 2013)

14.52.090 Parking meters, pay stations and parking meter/pay station standards
not to be used for certain purposes.

A. Single space meters. It is unlawful for any person to attach anything to or allow a
bicycle, newsrack or any other article or thing to lean against a parking meter or a
parking meter standard.

B. Pay stations. It is unlawful for any person to attach anything to or allow a bicycle,
newsrack or any other article or thing to lean against a pay station unit or a pay station
standard. (Ord. 7305-NS (part), 2013)

14.52.100 Rule of evidence.

A. Single space meters. The parking or standing of any motor vehicle in a parking
space, at which space the parking meter displays the sign or signal indicating illegal
parking, shall constitute a prima facie presumption that the vehicle has been parked or
allowed to stand in such space for a period longer than permitted by this chapter.

B. Pay-and-display stations. The parking or standing of any motor vehicle in a parking
space, at which space the pay-and-display station dispensing machine ticket indicates
illegal parking, shall constitute a prima facie presumption that the vehicle has been
parked or allowed to stand in such space for a period longer than permitted by this
chapter.

C. Pay-by-plate stations. The parking or standing of any motor vehicle in a parking
space, at which space the vehicle license plate has not been registered at the nearest
pay-by-plate station, shall constitute a prima facie presumption that the vehicle has
been parked or allowed to stand in such a space for a period longer than permitted by
this chapter.

  14.52.110 Use of money deposited in parking meters and pay stations.

  Except as permitted under subdivision G below, all moneys collected from parking
meters and pay stations in the City shall be placed in a special fund, which fund shall be
used for the following purposes:
                                     Page 29 of 518




A. For the purchasing, leasing, installing, repairing, maintaining, operating, removing,
regulating and policing of parking meters and pay stations in the City and for the
payment of any and all expenses relating or incidental thereto.

B. For the purchasing, leasing, acquiring, improving, operating and maintaining of off-
street parking facilities in the City.

C. For the installation and maintenance of traffic control devices and signals.

D. For the painting and marking of streets and curbs required for the direction of traffic
and the parking of motor vehicles.

E. For the proper regulation, control and inspection of parking and traffic upon the
public streets.

F. To be pledged as security for the payment of principal of and interest on off-street
parking revenue bonds issued by the City.

G. Additional Revenue deemed to be generated by the goBerkeley Program will be
used to fund goBerkeley efforts, pursuant to Section 1012(b) of Intermodal Surface
Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991, as amended, as agreed in the 2012 Cooperative
Agreement between the City of Berkeley, the California Department of Transportation
and the Federal Highway Administration.

H. Surplus money not utilized under subdivision A through F above may be transferred
to the general fund. The City Manager or their designee may make an annual
determination as to what is surplus based on the needs and obligations of the special
fund and transfer such surplus to the general fund. (Ord. 7498-NS § 2, 2016: Ord. 7305-
NS (part), 2013).

  14.52.120 Parking meter and pay station fees.

  Single-space meter and pay station fees for the goBerkeley Program parking meter
zones hereinabove set forth in 14.52.010 shall be as follows:

  A. For goBerkeley Program parking meter zones set forth in 14.52.010:

1. Pay stations and credit card enabled single-space meters may accept nickels,
dimes, quarters, one dollar coins, credit/debit cards, and tap-to-pay mobile devices. The
City Manager may authorize the removal of coin-acceptance hardware to transition to a
cashless parking environment.

2. The minimum transaction amount for cash payment shall be five cents ($0.05) and
shall purchase a segment of time proportional to the prevailing hourly rate, rounded up
                                      Page 30 of 518




to the nearest whole minute. The prevailing hourly rate for meter zones specified
in 14.52.010 shall be set by section 14.52.120(B).

3. The minute minimum transaction amount for credit/debit card payment shall be set
by the City Manager to ensure cost recovery for transaction processing fees. The
prevailing hourly rate for meter zones specified in 14.52.010 shall be set by
section 14.52.120(B).

 B. At single-space meters and pay stations within the goBerkeley Program parking
meter zones:

1. The hourly rate may vary between $0.50 and $5.00 per hour effective FY 2017,
between $0.50 and $6.00 per hour effective FY 2018, between $0.50 and $7.00
effective FY 2019, and between $0.50 and $8.00 effective FY 2020, as set by the City
Manager.

2. The parking fee may be either flat rates (same rate for a specified time period e.g. 1
hour, 4 hours, all day), or may be variable rates based on time of day, length of stay, or
a combination of those pricing structures, as set by the City Manager.

3. The City Manager may adjust the parking fee by increments no larger than 50 cents
($0.50) per hour.

4. The City Manager may implement special event pricing at designated times and at
designated pay stations and parking meters,

5. Adjustments to the parking fee must be supported by published data on parking
usage statistics with the goal of achieving 65-85% parking occupancy of spaces as
calculated in the goBerkeley Program Guidelines.

6. Adjustments to the parking fee at pay stations and parking meters must be posted to
the City’s website no later than 30 calendar days prior to the adjustment.

7. Parking rates may be adjusted no more frequently than once per 60 calendar
days. (Ord. 7752-NS § 2, 2021: Ord. 7498-NS § 3, 2016: Ord. 7308-NS § 1, 2013: Ord.
7305-NS (part), 2013)

14.52.130 Time limits enforced at inoperable parking meters and pay stations.

A. Single space meters. Where parking meters are installed in the City, if the parking
meter is inoperable, the time limits posted on the parking meter shall be enforced during
the hours of operation of parking meters.

B. Pay stations. Where pay stations are installed in the City, if the pay station is
inoperable, the time limits posted on the pay station within the block that the vehicle is
                                    Page 31 of 518




parked or indicated by signage or curb markings shall be enforced during the hours of
operation of the pay station.

                             RESOLUTION NO. ##,###-N.S.

   DIRECTING THE CITY MANAGER TO TRANSITION FROM CITY-ABSORBED
  PARKING METER TRANSACTION COSTS TO A TRANSPARENT TRANSACTION
                   CHARGE PAID BY THE CUSTOMER

WHEREAS, the City of Berkeley’s goBerkeley Parking Management Program is
designed to manage curb space through demand-responsive pricing; and

WHEREAS, the Parking Meter Fund (631) and Off-Street Parking Fund (627) are
currently facing projected structural deficits due to rising operational, maintenance, and
personnel costs; and

WHEREAS, the City currently utilizes a “hidden fee” model for on-street parking and
garage transactions, wherein the City absorbs all credit card processing fees and
merchant service charges, effectively reducing the net revenue available for
infrastructure maintenance and operational improvements; and

WHEREAS, the absorption of these fees results in a multi-hundred-thousand-dollar
annual impact on the Parking Meter Fund; and

WHEREAS, Berkeley’s existing mobile payment platform (ParkMobile) already utilizes a
transparent service fee model, wherein the customer pays a small “convenience” fee for
the convenience of mobile payment, a model that is widely accepted and understood by
the public; and

WHEREAS, transitioning to a transparent transaction charge for all credit card and
digital transactions at physical meters and pay stations will align Berkeley’s hardware
payment model with its mobile payment model, creating a consistent user experience
across all payment platforms; and

WHEREAS, this shift ensures that the costs of digital payment processing are borne by
the user of the service rather than being subsidized by the City’s parking funds, thereby
preserving revenue for critical public services and transit-related goals; and

WHEREAS, providing transparency in cost structures allows the City to more accurately
set hourly parking rates based on occupancy data without those rates being artificially
inflated or eroded by merchant service costs; and

WHEREAS, the City Council finds this action is exempt from the California
Environmental Quality Act pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15301, 15307 and
15308.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Berkeley that the
City Manager is hereby authorized and directed to transition the City’s parking payment
                                    Page 35 of 518




systems from a City-absorbed cost model to a transparent transaction charge model,
wherein a per-transaction service charge is paid by the customer.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the City Manager is authorized to set and adjust
such costs as necessary to cover the prevailing costs of credit card processing and
vendor transaction charges, ensuring the model remains consistent with the City’s
mobile payment integrations.
                                     Page 36 of 518




                            RESOLUTION NO. ##,###-N.S.

      ADOPTING A NEW FEE STRUCTURE AND UPDATING FEES FOR THE
      RESIDENTIAL PARKING PERMIT (RPP) PROGRAM TO ACHIEVE COST
          RECOVERY AND ADVANCE CITY ENVIRONMENTAL GOALS

WHEREAS, the Residential Parking Permit (RPP) Program was established in 1980 to
protect Berkeley neighborhoods from commuter parking overflow and to preserve the
quality of life for residents; and

WHEREAS, the annual cost to administer, maintain, and enforce the RPP program—
including personnel costs for Public Works administrative staff, 21 Police Department
Parking Enforcement Officers, and 3 supervisors—is approximately $4.12 million; and

WHEREAS, the RPP program has historically operated at a significant structural deficit,
with average annual permit revenues of only $2.85 million, requiring a $1.3 million
annual subsidy from the City’s General Fund and Parking Meter Fund; and

WHEREAS, the City’s Strategic Plan and Climate Action Plan prioritize the efficient
management of the public right-of-way and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions
through sustainable transportation policies; and

WHEREAS, the current "flat-fee" permit structure does not account for the
disproportionate impact of households that store three or more private vehicles on
public streets, which limits available curb space for other residents and service
providers; and

WHEREAS, a graduated fee structure—wherein the cost of each subsequent permit at
a single address increases—is a proven management tool to encourage the use of off-
street parking, reduce the "privatization" of public space for long-term vehicle storage,
and promote alternative modes of transportation; and

WHEREAS, the City Council finds it necessary to adjust RPP fees to move the program
toward a self-sustaining "enterprise" model, ensuring that the beneficiaries of the
program cover the costs of its operation and enforcement.

WHEREAS, the City Council finds this action is exempt from the California
Environmental Quality Act pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15307 and 15308.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Berkeley that the
City Manager is hereby authorized to update the Residential Parking Permit fee
schedule to reflect a graduated pricing model.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the new fee structure shall be implemented effective
July 1, 2027 (FY 2028), as follows:

                            RESOLUTION NO. ##,###-N.S.

ADOPTING AN UPDATED SCHEDULE OF FINES AND LATE PAYMENT PENALTIES
   FOR PARKING VIOLATIONS TO ENSURE REGIONAL ALIGNMENT, COST
 RECOVERY, AND ENFORCEMENT EFFICACY; AND RESCINDING RESOLUTION
                          NO. 71,627-N.S.

WHEREAS, the current fine amounts for most parking violations have not been adjusted
in over 15 years, failing to keep pace with the rising costs of personnel, equipment, and
the specialized technology required for modern parking enforcement; and

WHEREAS, while the majority of Berkeley’s parking fine amounts were last updated in
2010, the schedule of fines was expanded to include new violation types in 2012, 2018,
2023, and 2024; and

WHEREAS, an analysis of neighboring jurisdictions reveals that Berkeley’s current fines
are significantly lower than those of Oakland and San Francisco—for example,
Berkeley’s $43 expired meter fine is approximately 33% lower than Oakland’s $64 fine
and over 100% lower than San Francisco’s $108 fine—thereby diminishing the deterrent
effect of citations; and

WHEREAS, when parking fines are low relative to the cost of off-street parking or the
value of convenience, drivers are more likely to risk illegal parking, which increases
double-parking, blocks bike lanes, and prevents the target occupancy of 65-85%
necessary for a healthy parking management program; and

WHEREAS, a 3-49% increase in the amount of each parking fine, based on cumulative
inflation occurring since the year a particular fine was last updated, based on the
Consumer Price Index (CPI), will bring Berkeley into closer alignment with regional
standards while ensuring that the cost of managing the public right-of-way is supported
by those who violate established regulations; and

WHEREAS, the City Council finds that increasing these penalties is necessary to
reinforce the deterrent effect of citations, encourage compliance with the goBerkeley
program guidelines, and keep pace with the rising costs to the City of implementing the
program; and

WHEREAS, the City Council finds this action is exempt from the California
Environmental Quality Act pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Sections 15301, 15307 and
15308.

NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Berkeley that the
Schedule of Parking Violations and Fines and the Schedule of Late Payment Penalties
are hereby amended to increase all existing fine and penalty amounts by 3-49%,
rounded to the nearest whole dollar.
                                    Page 39 of 518




BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this updated schedule shall take effect on May 1,
2026, and the City Manager is authorized to take all necessary administrative actions to
update enforcement software and public notification materials accordingly.

                   NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING
                    BERKELEY CITY COUNCIL
    PREFERENTIAL PARKING PROGRAM PERMIT FEES AND PARKING
                   METER TRANSACTION FEES

     The public may participate in this hearing by remote video or in-person.

Notice is hereby given by the City Council of the City of Berkeley that a public hearing
will be conducted by said city council of the City of Berkeley at which time and place all
persons may attend and be heard upon the following:

The Department of Public Works is proposing to increase the Preferential Parking
Program permit fees and charge parking meter transaction fees to reduce the RPP and
goBerkeley programs’ operational deficit and recover program costs.

The hearing will be held on May 19, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. in the School District Board Room,
located at 1231 Addison Street, Berkeley CA 94702.

For further information, please contact at Elliott Schwimmer, Senior Planner,
510.981.7066.

A copy of the agenda material for this hearing will be available on the City’s website at
https://berkeleyca.gov/ as of 5:00 p.m. on May 7, 2026. Once posted, the agenda for
this meeting will include a link for public participation using Zoom video
technology, as well as any health and safety requirements for in-person
attendance.

Written comments should be mailed or delivered directly to the City Clerk, 2180 Milvia
Street, Berkeley, CA 94704, or e-mailed to council@berkeleyca.gov in order to ensure
delivery to all Councilmembers and inclusion in the agenda packet.

Communications to the Berkeley City Council are public record and will become part of
the City’s electronic records, which are accessible through the City’s website. Please
note: e-mail addresses, names, addresses, and other contact information are not
required, but if included in any communication to the City Council, will become
part of the public record. If you do not want your e-mail address or any other contact
information to be made public, you may deliver communications via U.S. Postal Service
or in person to the City Clerk. If you do not want your contact information included in
the public record, please do not include that information in your communication. Please
contact the City Clerk at (510) 981-6900 or clerk@cityofberkeley.info for further
information.

If you challenge the above in court, you may be limited to raising only those issues you
or someone else raised at the public hearing described in this notice, or in written
correspondence delivered to the City of Berkeley at, or prior to, the public hearing.
Background information concerning this proposal will be available at the City Clerk
                                     Page 518 of 518




Department and posted on the City of Berkeley webpage at least 12 days prior to the
public hearing.

Published: May 1 and May 8, 2026 – The Berkeley Voice
Published pursuant to Government Code Section 6062a
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
I hereby certify that the Notice for this Public Hearing of the Berkeley City Council was
posted at the display case located near the walkway in front of the Maudelle Shirek
Building, 2134 Martin Luther King Jr. Way, as well as on the City’s website, on May 7,
2026.
